title: Interop smoke test against a real ACP client over stdio
description:
The verification that cannot be faked by our own test suite: a client we did not write completes a session against python-acp over stdio.

Options are the SDK's own example clients under examples/, or a real editor integration (Zed, Neovim). Prefer something runnable in CI; if nothing is, make it a documented manual procedure with recorded output rather than skipping it.

This is the payoff for decision D2 -- it is the check that 'strict full ACP v1' means something outside this repository.
acceptance_criteria: A third-party ACP client completes initialize, session creation, a prompt turn with streamed updates, and clean shutdown against python-acp over stdio; the procedure is automated in CI or documented as a manual runbook with recorded output; failures are diagnosable from the captured transcript.
notes: pyacp-tzd.2 delivered the stdio binding and a subprocess-level test (tests/test_transport_stdio.py) that drives 'python -m python_acp.cli --transport stdio' with the SDK's own ClientSideConnection via acp.stdio.spawn_agent_process. That covers startup, JSON-RPC framing over a pipe, initialize, and clean exit - but the client is the SDK's, not a third party's, and no session is created because session/new is still -32601 until pyacp-3rw.2. This bead remains the real-client, full-session check.
close_reason: Two halves. AUTOMATED: tests/interop/acp_client.py runs as its own process importing only acp (asserted via AST), completing initialize/session-new-with-own-MCP-server/tool-running prompt/refused prompt/list/close/clean-exit over a pipe; tests/test_interop.py asserts the recorded transcript. RECORDED: the SDK's examples/client.py driven against us, transcript and upstream commit in docs/interop.md, with the honest note that it hardcodes mcp_servers=[] so it cannot reach a tool. FINDING: the SDK's reference client refuses session/request_permission, which pyacp-8bv.1 treated as a broken client and refused the turn for -- reproduced, corrected to proceed-and-announce, and scoped to this executor because an LLM-backed one would need the decision remade. 478 tests.

title: Build the method-by-method ACP conformance suite
description:
Test every method in Phase 0.2's compliance matrix against its disposition: implemented methods behave per spec, declined methods return the correct error. The matrix is the checklist; a method absent from the suite is a gap in the matrix or the suite.

Structure it so adding an Agent method without adding conformance coverage is visibly incomplete. This suite is what makes the Phase 7 removal safe, so it must be trustworthy before that lands.
acceptance_criteria: Every Agent method in the matrix has conformance coverage matching its disposition; declined methods are asserted to return the correct error, not merely to fail; the suite runs under make test on all four matrix Python versions; a new method with no coverage is detectable.
notes: pyacp-4ns.2: cases derive mechanically from docs/acp-compliance-matrix.md, including the declines. See its 'What Phase 8 tests' section - notably the both-directions test for the three unstable-gated methods, and pinning -32601 for session/delete, logout, providers/*, nes/*, and document/* so a future SDK bump that starts routing them is noticed.
close_reason: tests/test_conformance.py: 62 cases from one CONFORMANCE table covering all 15 Agent members. Declines assert the correct error (-32601 with data.method; -32000 for authenticate), unstable three tested both directions, 16 unrouted AGENT_METHODS names pinned as unregistered, and every advertised capability mapped to the method it promises and called. Gap detection verified by deleting a row (4 tests catch it). Cross-version bug found and fixed: Agent.__protocol_attrs__ is 3.12+ and empty on 3.11, so the member walk passed vacuously on the project floor; replaced with vars(Agent) and pinned. 470 tests pass on 3.11 and 3.14.

title: Call session/request_permission from the turn executor
description:
CORRECTION FROM THE ORIGINAL PLAN: request_permission is an acp.interfaces.Client method. The agent CALLS it; it does not implement it. The original plan's 'Implement session/request_permission' was backwards.

Before a consequential tool call, ask the client for permission with the tool call and the available PermissionOptions, and honor the answer. Handle the cancellation outcome -- the client can cancel the turn while the permission prompt is open, which must land as stopReason cancelled (Phase 3.5), not as a denied permission.

Evaluate acp.contrib.permissions, which ships a permission broker.
acceptance_criteria: The executor requests permission before consequential tool calls and honors allow, deny, and always-variants; cancellation while a prompt is open produces stopReason cancelled; behavior when the client does not support permissions is defined and tested; which tool calls are consequential is documented; whether acp.contrib.permissions is used is recorded with a reason.
notes:
pyacp-hnk.1: session/request_permission has NO capability gate -- ClientCapabilities has no field for it and every ACP client must accept it. Do not add one to turns.Gate. Call it straight off context.client.
CORRECTED by pyacp-6ni.4. This bead decided a client answering -32601 to
session/request_permission was broken and refused the turn. The SDK's own
examples/client.py answers exactly that, and the interop run reproduced the failure: a
well-formed tool invocation came back stopReason refusal with the tool never run.

New behaviour: the turn PROCEEDS and announces it once per session via an
agent_message_chunk. The client named the tool and arguments in session/prompt itself, so
the authorization already exists -- the prompt was a courtesy to a human who might be
watching, and a client that cannot reach one has already decided.

SCOPE: this reasoning is specific to the deterministic tool router. An LLM-backed executor
CHOOSES the tool, so a client's prompt authorizes nothing in particular and the same
fallback would be a hole. Any executor added later must decide it again. Stated at the
fallback in turn_mcp_router.py and in docs/interop.md.
close_reason: The router calls session/request_permission before every tool call (all calls are consequential: MCP 2024-11-05 has no tool annotations, follow-up filed). Denial vs cancellation kept distinct -- DeniedOutcome's literal is 'cancelled', so a reject option marks the call failed and continues while a cancelled outcome returns stopReason cancelled without raising CancelledError (agent.prompt reads turn.cancelled(), and a raised CancelledError would leave the request unanswered). always-variants remembered on the Session, copied by fork. A client refusing the mandatory method gets a refusal. acp.contrib.permissions.PermissionBroker USED; its default option set is missing reject_always so we add the fourth. 407 tests; verified against a real ACP client over stdio.

title: Get stopReason semantics right, especially cancelled
description:
prompt must return the correct stopReason for every exit path: normal completion, cancellation, refusal, and any limit condition the executor can hit.

'cancelled' is called out in the plan's verification because it is the one most easily got wrong -- a cancelled turn must return the response with stopReason cancelled, not raise, not hang, and not return end_turn. It also has to interleave correctly with in-flight session/update notifications and with an MCP call still running in the backend.

Pairs with Phase 1.5's $/cancel_request registry; these are two different cancellation mechanisms and both must be verified.
acceptance_criteria: Each exit path returns its correct stopReason; cancelling mid-turn returns stopReason cancelled promptly rather than raising or hanging; no session/update notifications are emitted after the turn response; an in-flight MCP call is cancelled or abandoned cleanly; tests cover cancel-before-start, cancel-mid-tool-call, and cancel-after-completion.
notes:
pyacp-hnk.1 completed the seam in src/python_acp/turns.py. What is now there:
- TurnExecutor: async execute(context, prompt) -> TurnResult. Single method, async, no
  step count and no rule against client round-trips mid-turn, so multi-step/interactive
  turns are open by construction (held by test_a_turn_may_be_multi_step_and_interactive).
- TurnResult(stop_reason, usage=None), TurnResult.ended(). agent.prompt fills
  PromptResponse.usage from it. The type can already express all five stopReasons.
- TurnContext: session, client, session_id, emit(update), gates, allows(gate),
  require(gate), cancelled, wait_for_cancellation(). emit supplies the session id itself
  and records into Session.history for session/load replay; it is UNGATED on purpose.
- Gate / ClientGates / UngatedClientCallError (a RuntimeError -> -32603, because an
  ungated call is OUR conformance bug, not a bad parameter). Three gate shapes that are
  not interchangeable: fs is two independent booleans; terminal is one boolean for all
  five terminal/* methods; plan and elicitation are advertised by PRESENCE (empty marker
  models, so `is not None`, never bool(model)). session/update and
  session/request_permission have NO gate -- do not invent one.
- Cancellation: Session.cancellation is set BEFORE the task is cancelled, so inside an
  `except CancelledError` an executor can tell session/cancel from the request dying, and
  can run cleanup under asyncio.shield. Let CancelledError propagate; agent.py turns a
  cancelled turn into stopReason "cancelled".
Full rationale in src/python_acp/turns.md.
pyacp-8bv.1: there are now TWO routes to stopReason cancelled and both must keep working. (1) session/cancel cancels the turn task -> agent.prompt sees turn.cancelled() and answers cancelled. (2) The client answers a permission request with DeniedOutcome (whose literal is 'cancelled', NOT denied) -> McpToolRouterExecutor returns TurnResult('cancelled') directly, without any task cancellation. Route 2 is why the executor does not raise asyncio.CancelledError itself: agent.prompt checks turn.cancelled(), which would be False, and a raised CancelledError is a BaseException the SDK does not catch, so the request would never be answered. Also: RequestPermissionResponse.outcome is AllowedOutcome('selected'+optionId) | DeniedOutcome('cancelled'). Denial is a SELECTED reject option; the only non-selected answer is cancellation. Reading DeniedOutcome as a rejection turns a 'no' into stopReason cancelled.

pyacp-tzd.5 closed as superseded (2026-08-23): $/cancel_request is not an ACP method -- verified against the upstream schema sources (agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol main, agent-client-protocol-schema/src/v1/), where the only cancellation is the session/cancel notification. SDK 0.12.1's CancelRequestNotification (acp/schema.py:2636) is an orphan model: no AGENT_METHODS/CLIENT_METHODS entry, absent from the ClientNotification params union, referenced nowhere, no wire name. So this bead is the ONLY cancellation work, and the description's "Pairs with Phase 1.5's $/cancel_request registry; these are two different cancellation mechanisms and both must be verified" is void -- there is no second mechanism.

The MCP-side half already exists, from pyacp-ua1 (on main): MCPStdioClient.cancel_request(request_id, reason=None) sends notifications/cancelled. It never raises (catches MCPProtocolError and OSError, because _write reaches drain() and a subprocess dying mid-write throws BrokenPipeError), and it deliberately does not touch _pending -- whoever abandoned the request owns that future. Use it for this bead's "an in-flight MCP call is cancelled or abandoned cleanly" criterion. request() already calls it on timeout, skipping initialize only.
close_reason: All five acceptance criteria met; merged to main. Both routes to cancelled pinned by an evidence map; max_tokens/max_turn_requests DECLINED with structural reasons (no LLM, no agent-initiated request loop). 563 tests pass.

title: Ship the deterministic MCP tool-router turn executor
description:
The default executor: interpret prompt content blocks as explicit MCP tool invocations, run them against the session's MCP backends, stream real tool_call and tool_call_update notifications, and return end_turn. No reasoning, no model.

Define and document the input convention -- how a content block names a tool and carries arguments -- since this is the contract every client of this executor codes against, and it is invented here rather than given by the spec.

Decide the behavior for prompts that do not parse as a tool invocation: error, or a message chunk explaining the convention.
acceptance_criteria: Prompt content mapped to MCP tool calls by a documented convention; tool_call and tool_call_update notifications carry real status transitions and results; multiple tool calls in one turn work; unparseable prompts produce a defined, tested outcome; end_turn returned on success; the convention is documented in the README and the module doc.
notes:

  client it gets is live. Opening is all-or-nothing; a session whose servers failed does

title: Define the TurnExecutor interface
description:
Decision D3's seam. Define the interface a prompt turn runs behind: it receives the session and its content blocks, may call client methods (Phase 4), emits session/update notifications, and returns a stopReason.

This is what makes 'no LLM in the loop' a design choice rather than a dead end, and it satisfies the original Phase 6.3 'backend abstraction for non-MCP executors' in the same stroke.

Design it so an LLM-backed executor is droppable in later without reopening the interface -- specifically, do not assume the turn is synchronous, single-step, or free of client round-trips.
acceptance_criteria: A documented TurnExecutor interface with streaming update emission, client-method access, cancellation, and stopReason return; the deterministic executor and at least one test double both implement it; the interface does not assume a single-step or non-interactive turn; sibling .md written; the seam is reflected in ARCHITECTURE.md.
notes:
pyacp-3rw.2 seeded src/python_acp/turns.py because this bead depends on it and
session/prompt had to be wired to something; putting a provisional seam in agent.py would
have violated module-boundaries (agent.py is method-shaped translation only). Recorded as
decision B6b.

What is there: TurnExecutor Protocol with one `async execute(context, prompt) -> StopReason`;
TurnContext(session, client) exposing session_id and `emit(update)` (which supplies the
session id itself so an executor cannot address another session); IdleTurnExecutor, the
default that completes a turn having done nothing and logs a warning.

Because the call is async and single-method, nothing assumes the turn is synchronous,
single-step, or free of client round-trips -- this bead's stated constraint.

What this bead must STILL add (also listed in src/python_acp/turns.md):
- stopReason beyond end_turn/cancelled: max_tokens, max_turn_requests, refusal (hnk.5)
- capability-gated client-method access; context.client is the raw facade today
- a cancellation token, so an executor can run async cleanup without racing the cancel
- content-block typing; `prompt` is list[Any] and the promptCapabilities literals stay
  false in AGENT_CAPABILITY_MANIFEST until hnk.3 enforces them
- a TurnResult carrying usage; PromptResponse.usage exists and nothing fills it

agent.py already owns the cancelled path: the turn runs as its own task and
asyncio.wait({turn}) + turn.cancelled() distinguishes "session/cancel reached it" from
"this request was cancelled". Do not change that to `await turn` -- it makes the two
indistinguishable.
close_reason: turns.py completed: TurnExecutor Protocol (one async method, multi-step/interactive open by construction and held by a design test), TurnResult carrying stopReason+usage, TurnContext with emit/gates/cancellation, Gate+ClientGates+UngatedClientCallError (-32603), and Session.cancellation set BEFORE task cancellation so an executor can tell session/cancel from a dead request. turns.md rewritten; ARCHITECTURE seam updated; seams recorded on hnk.2/4/5 and 8bv.1-4. Two implementers exercise the interface (IdleTurnExecutor + test doubles); the deterministic executor is hnk.2's and will be the third. 329 tests pass.

title: Implement the baseline session lifecycle: new_session, prompt, cancel, session_update
description:
The minimum viable ACP session: create one, prompt it, stream updates back, cancel it. This is the path a real client exercises first and the one Phase 8's interop smoke test depends on.

prompt's body is Phase 3's turn executor -- here, wire the plumbing and the session/update emission channel, not the turn semantics.

session/cancel must cooperatively stop the running turn; the stopReason 'cancelled' contract is Phase 3.5.
acceptance_criteria: new_session creates a registry entry and returns a valid NewSessionResponse; prompt dispatches to the turn executor and streams session/update notifications to the client; cancel stops an in-flight turn; a client can run the full create-prompt-cancel cycle over stdio; tests cover each step and the cancel-with-no-turn-running case.
notes:
pyacp-3rw.1 built the registry this bead wires up. Seams already in place:
- SessionRegistry.create(cwd, additional_directories=, modes=, config_options=, title=)
  returns a Session; agent.py should hold ONE registry per process (not per connection --
  it is shared across WebSocket connections so a disconnect cannot delete a session another
  connection may resume).
- Session.attach_turn(task) / detach_turn() / cancel_turn() is where session/cancel reaches.
  attach_turn raises TurnAlreadyRunningError (-> -32603) on a second concurrent prompt;
  cancel_turn() returns False for an idle session, which is NOT an error (session/cancel is
  a notification and a client cancelling a finished turn is behaving correctly).
- UnknownSessionError subclasses ValueError, so errors.to_request_error already maps a
  stale sessionId to -32602 with the id in data.reason. No special case needed.
- Path validation is deliberately absent from the registry; pyacp-3rw.4 owns it at the edge.
close_reason: new_session/prompt/cancel live against SessionRegistry; turns.py seeded with the TurnExecutor seam (decision B6b, hnk.1 completes it); IdleTurnExecutor as the honest default. Turn runs as a task so session/cancel reaches it; asyncio.wait+turn.cancelled() distinguishes turn-cancelled from request-cancelled. One registry per process, required on the agent. session/new rejects unadvertised MCP transports. Full create-prompt-cancel cycle verified over a spawned stdio process and over WebSocket. 234 tests pass.

title: Build the session registry with cwd, additionalDirectories, mode, config, and timestamps
description:
There is no session concept in the runtime at all -- session/* currently returns -32601. Introduce a registry holding, per session: id, cwd, additionalDirectories, current mode, config option state, creation and last-activity timestamps, and the handle to its MCP backend(s).

Evaluate acp.contrib.session_state before writing one; the SDK ships a session accumulator that may cover most of this.

Session state is what makes fork_session and resume_session meaningful in Phase 2.4, so decide the copy-versus-share semantics for backends and history here rather than later.
acceptance_criteria: A session registry exists with the full metadata set; sessions are addressable by id; lifetime is defined (creation, expiry or explicit close, cleanup of backends on close); copy-versus-share semantics for fork and resume are documented; whether acp.contrib.session_state is used or replaced is recorded with a reason; the new module ships its sibling .md.
close_reason: sessions.py + sessions.md + 35 tests. acp.contrib.session_state evaluated and replaced (client-side accumulator, single-session, no metadata, experimental) with the reason recorded in the module doc; noted as the right tool for load_session history on pyacp-3rw.3. Fork=deep copy/own backends/starts idle, resume=shares, documented and tested. Lifetime: no idle expiry, explicit close, on_close hook as the mcp_registry seam (module-boundaries B6a). 214 tests pass.

title: Add a request registry and cooperative cancellation for $/cancel_request
description:
There is no cancellation anywhere in the runtime today. Add a per-connection registry of in-flight requests and cooperative cancellation driven by $/cancel_request, so a client can abandon work rather than wait out a timeout.

Distinct from session/cancel (Phase 3.5), which cancels a prompt turn and must produce stopReason 'cancelled'. This one cancels an individual JSON-RPC request. Both must work; they are different mechanisms and the plan's verification calls for both to be tested.

Interacts with pyacp-ua1: when a cancelled request has an MCP call in flight, the backend should be told via notifications/cancelled rather than left computing a reply nobody reads.
acceptance_criteria: In-flight requests are tracked per connection and cancellable by id; $/cancel_request cancels cooperatively without killing the connection or sibling requests; a cancelled request produces the correct ACP error; cancellation propagates to an in-flight MCP call; tests cover cancelling mid-flight, cancelling an unknown id, and cancelling an already-completed request.
notes:
pyacp-4ns.3 finding: grep of SDK 0.12.1 meta.py, connection.py, and router.py turns up no route or constant for $/cancel_request anywhere. AGENT_METHODS carries session/cancel only. So either $/cancel_request is ours to add (likely via ext_method plus our own request registry) or the requirement is stale. Confirm against acp.interfaces under pyacp-4ns.2 before starting.
pyacp-4ns.2 re-confirmed against the installed 0.12.1: no $/cancel_request route exists in acp/meta.py, acp/router.py, or acp/agent/router.py. ACP cancellation is the session/cancel notification (CancelNotification -> Agent.cancel), which pyacp-3rw.2 and pyacp-hnk.5 already cover. Either this bead means the JSON-RPC-level cancel and must build it on ext_method, or it is a misreading of the spec and should be closed against session/cancel. Decide before implementing.

pyacp-tzd.6 finding, for the "$/cancel_request has no home" question: acp.schema.Error accepts -32800 in its code literal union, alongside the six JSON-RPC standard codes and ACP's -32000/-32002. acp.RequestError supplies NO constructor for it and the schema carries no description; it appears nowhere else in the SDK. -32800 is LSP's RequestCancelled, which ACP's error shape otherwise mirrors. Could not confirm against upstream ACP docs (schema/rust sources 404 at the URLs tried). errors.py now exposes REQUEST_CANCELLED = -32800 and request_cancelled(reason=None) on that reading, with the uncertainty documented in errors.md; confirm before putting it on the wire. Also settled by tzd.6: asyncio.CancelledError is never mapped to a RequestError -- to_request_error re-raises it, because returning a value from a cancelled coroutine tells asyncio the cancellation did not take. Whatever reports a cancellation must do so after letting the exception propagate.
close_reason: Superseded: $/cancel_request is not an ACP method. Verified against upstream agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol main (agent-client-protocol-schema/src/v1/agent.rs, client.rs, rpc.rs, ext.rs): the only cancellation in the protocol is the session/cancel notification (SESSION_CANCEL_METHOD_NAME). The SDK 0.12.1 CancelRequestNotification model at acp/schema.py:2636 is an orphan -- no AGENT_METHODS/CLIENT_METHODS entry, not in the ClientNotification params union, referenced nowhere in the SDK, and no wire name exists for it anywhere. Prior notes (pyacp-4ns.2/.3) reached the same suspicion from the SDK routing tables alone; this closes it against upstream. Turn cancellation is pyacp-hnk.5; telling the MCP backend to stop is MCPStdioClient.cancel_request() from pyacp-ua1, wired from the session/cancel path per hnk.5 acceptance criteria. docs/full-apc-plan.md 1.5 and Verification item 2 corrected in the same change.

title: Implement initialize negotiation with accurate capabilities and auth methods
description:
Today's initialize returns a hand-built block of literals: loadSession false, promptCapabilities all false, mcpCapabilities http/sse false, auth.logout null, sessionCapabilities delete/additionalDirectories null, authMethods empty. The acp-protocol skill is explicit that this block is a PROMISE, not a reflection of runtime state.

Rebuild it from Phase 0.2's compliance matrix using the SDK's InitializeResponse model, and capture the incoming clientCapabilities -- Phase 4 gates every client call on them, so they must be stored per-connection and reachable from the turn executor.

_SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1 is the ACP version and is unrelated to the MCP protocolVersion string in MCPStdioClient.initialize. Two protocols, two version fields; do not merge them.

title: Support runtime-configured MCP servers via session/new mcpServers

title: acp-protocol skill error table and 'Known constraints' section are stale
description:
Two separate staleness problems in .claude/skills/acp-protocol/SKILL.md, both predating and now compounded by pyacp-k5w.

1. The error-code mapping table says 'MCP backend failed -> -32603, raised as MCPProtocolError'. As of pyacp-k5w that is only half true: an MCPProtocolError carrying a server-assigned code now forwards that code, and -32603 is the fallback for codeless failures. The table needs the extra row and the data.source convention.

2. The 'Known constraints in the MCP backend' section is factually wrong about code that has since changed: it claims _read_response discards non-matching ids (the module has had a full _read_loop with a pending-future map for a while) and that 'start() pipes stderr but nothing drains it' (_drain_stderr exists and is load-bearing). pyacp-4ns.4 rewrites this skill for the SDK contract and may absorb both, but item 2 is wrong today regardless of the SDK migration and item 1 is a live contradiction between skill and code.

title: Final architecture and module documentation refresh
description:
The consistency pass, run once the module boundaries have stopped moving. Documentation is no longer a phase of its own -- the original Phase 7 workstream is complete and repo-docs-sync enforces co-located docs per change -- so this issue only closes the drift that accumulates across eight phases of refactoring.

Check specifically: ARCHITECTURE.md's two Mermaid diagrams against the delivered module layout, every sibling .md against its module's actual symbols, README links, and the mermaid rendering itself. Use the repo-docs-sync skill.

Original plan Further Consideration 2 suggested a CI check for markdown link integrity and mermaid syntax; decide here whether to file it.
acceptance_criteria: Both ARCHITECTURE.md diagrams match the delivered architecture; every production module has a current sibling .md naming real symbols; no broken cross-links; mermaid renders; the CI link and mermaid check is either filed as a follow-up issue or explicitly declined.
close_reason:
Phase 8's consistency pass. ARCHITECTURE.md: merged the 'Subsystems Today' and 'Target Subsystems (ACP v1)' sections into one -- the second was a strict subset of the first and its prose was badly stale ('session and prompt methods answer -32601 until Phases 2 and 3', 'the capability block is entirely off', 'the agent cannot reach the MCP backend yet', all false). Its initialize sequence diagram survives as a new 'The handshake' section, corrected. The delivered flowchart gained terminals.py, mcp_content.py, and the edges the router actually has.

Module docs: audited every public symbol against its sibling .md by AST walk -- two real gaps, sessions.PAGE_SIZE and turn_mcp_router.CommandRun, both now documented. Audited every test name cited in a doc: one hit, capabilities.md's test_phase_1_advertises_nothing, which turned out to be DELIBERATE history ('died with the first flip, as intended') -- and is the reason that check is not automated.

Further Consideration 2 (CI check for link integrity and mermaid syntax) is BUILT rather than filed: scripts/check_docs.py, wired to make docs-check and to CI, with tests/test_check_docs.py behind it because a gate that reports success by finding nothing fails open. It checks relative links resolve (from the linking file, not the root), every mermaid FLOWCHART edge names a node its own block defines with no duplicates, and the co-located doc rule. Deliberately narrower than 'mermaid syntax': it does not render (that needs node + headless browser) and does not follow #anchors (slugs are GitHub's business). The middle check is the one that matters -- GitHub renders a dangling edge as a plausible bare node rather than an error, which is exactly how the duplicate Router node survived.

repo-docs-sync skill rewritten around the automated check, with a 'what a green check still will not tell you' section for the audits that cannot be automated.

title: Add negative tests for unsupported methods, invalid params, and path constraints
description:
Cover the failure surface: unknown methods, malformed params, wrong types, missing required fields, relative paths, and paths outside the session's declared directories (Phase 2.5).

Each must produce the right error code, not merely fail. The current test suite asserts on specific JSON-RPC codes, and Phase 1.6 changes that mapping -- these tests are what verify the new mapping is coherent rather than accidental.
acceptance_criteria: Negative coverage for unknown methods, malformed and wrong-typed params, missing required fields, and both path-constraint violations; every case asserts the specific error code; the error codes match the mapping documented in the acp-protocol skill.
close_reason: Negative coverage for unknown methods, framing, non-object params, missing fields, wrong types, both path rules, unknown session ids, and authenticate; every case asserts its specific code; a table test proves nothing escapes the documented set or falls through to -32603. Filed pyacp-mej for the mcpServers salvage hole the suite made visible.

title: Add golden JSON-RPC transcript tests for initialize, lifecycle, streaming, and cancellation
description:
Record and assert full message transcripts for the four flows the plan's verification calls out, so ordering and payload-shape regressions surface as diffs rather than as mysterious client-side breakage.

Streaming and cancellation are where ordering actually matters: session/update notifications must not appear after the prompt response, and a cancelled turn has a specific message sequence. A transcript test catches that; a unit test typically does not.

Run transcripts over both transports if the framing differs between them.
acceptance_criteria: Golden transcripts for initialize, full session lifecycle, streaming updates, and cancellation; ordering assertions included, not just payload contents; transcripts regenerable by a documented command so intentional changes are cheap to accept; a reordering of notifications fails the suite.
close_reason: Golden transcripts for initialize, lifecycle, streaming, cancellation; ordering asserted by the golden diff AND by named invariants; regenerable via 'make transcripts' documented in Makefile/README/CLAUDE/AGENTS; a reordering is proven to fail the suite. Both transports covered at the level where they differ (stdio framing).

title: Emit deprecation warnings from the legacy action surface
description:
Decision D4's first step. The {"action": ...} surface -- list_tools, call_tool, list_prompts, get_prompt, list_resources, read_resource, ping, returning {ok: bool} envelopes -- keeps working, but every use now warns.

Warn on a channel a WebSocket client can actually see, not just the server log: a field in the response envelope is more useful to a consumer than a log line they never read. Decide and document the removal timeline so the warning can state it.
acceptance_criteria: Every legacy action logs a deprecation warning server-side and signals deprecation in the response envelope; the warning names the JSON-RPC replacement method and the removal milestone; existing action behavior is otherwise byte-identical; README marks the action surface deprecated with a migration table.
close_reason: Every action warns server-side (once per action per connection) and carries a 'deprecated' block naming replacement + milestone on success and failure alike; existing envelope keys untouched; README has the migration table. Milestone is a phase, not a version, per user decision. Passthrough left to sld.2.

title: Map MCP results onto ACP tool-call and content updates
description:
The translation layer between the two protocols, and the thing that makes the tool-router executor's streaming meaningful.

Map MCP tools/call results to ToolCallStart/ToolCallProgress payloads and MCP content types to ACP content blocks. The two protocols have overlapping but non-identical content models -- MCP text, image, audio, embedded resource, and resource link versus ACP's five block types -- so enumerate the mapping explicitly and decide what happens to anything unmappable.

Depends on pyacp-k5w for isError fidelity: a tool that failed must surface as a failed tool call, not a successful one carrying an error payload.
acceptance_criteria: An explicit, documented mapping table between MCP content types and ACP content blocks; MCP tool results drive correct ACP tool call status transitions; a tool returning isError true produces a failed tool call; unmappable content has a defined fallback; tests cover each content type.
notes: pyacp-hnk.2 shipped turn_mcp_router.py with a DELIBERATELY NARROW result mapping: _as_tool_content carries MCP text blocks through as ContentToolCallContent and SKIPS anything else rather than guessing, because a wrong 'type' on the wire is harder to notice than a missing block. This bead widens it -- images, embedded resources, resource links, annotations -- and should also decide whether a non-text MCP result block deserves a ToolCallContent variant or belongs in rawOutput (which already carries the whole result verbatim). Note ToolCallStart/Progress.content is a discriminated union of ContentToolCallContent | FileEditToolCallContent | TerminalToolCallContent; there is no diff variant under the name the plan assumed.
close_reason: mcp_content.py + .md + 23 tests: an explicit table for all five MCP content types (text/image/audio/embedded resource text+blob/resource_link) plus annotations. Unmappable content becomes a VISIBLE placeholder naming what it was and pointing at rawOutput, replacing hnk.2's skip -- once the mapping is complete a silent skip reads as 'the tool did nothing'. Same for a known type missing required fields. isError already drives status failed (k5w + hnk.2). Own module per decision B6e. Fixture gained an every-content tool so the mapping is tested against a real server; verified end-to-end over stdio. 501 tests.

title: Implement set_config_option for select and boolean variants, with config_option_update
description:
The SDK exposes this as one method taking either SetSessionConfigOptionBooleanRequest or SetSessionConfigOptionSelectRequest via @param_models, so one implementation handles both shapes -- do not write two.

Define the config options this runtime exposes, back them with the session registry's config state (Phase 2.1), and emit ConfigOptionUpdate on change. As with modes: only expose options that change behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Both request variants handled by one implementation; options are defined, advertised, and behaviorally meaningful; state persists in the session registry; ConfigOptionUpdate emitted on change; invalid config id and invalid value are rejected with the correct error; tests cover both variants.
notes: pyacp-hnk.4 recorded ConfigOptionUpdate as DEFERRED to this bead in turns.SESSION_UPDATE_DISPOSITIONS. Same three steps as fln.2: emit it after a successful Session.set_config_option (which already validates boolean-vs-select and the allowed values, including values nested in select GROUPS), flip the row from DEFERRED to EMITTED (test_the_deferred_variants_are_the_phase_5_ones will fail until you do), and note that nothing offers config options yet so NewSessionResponse.configOptions is None.
close_reason: One implementation for both request shapes (the SDK splats either into the same params; Session.set_config_option knows which value the named option takes). Two options with real behavioural differences: announce-tools (boolean, skips the per-turn tools/list) and on-tool-failure (select, continue|stop). stop leaves remaining plan entries pending because ACP has no stopReason for a failed tool. config_option_update via announce_config_options carrying every option. LAST unimplemented routed method: _not_implemented deleted, the three 'unbuilt' tests replaced with empty-set assertions rather than deleted, ConfigOptionUpdate flipped so no dispositions are DEFERRED. 530 tests; verified over stdio.

title: Implement set_session_mode and current_mode_update propagation
description:
Implement mode switching against the session registry's mode state (Phase 2.1), and emit CurrentModeUpdate when it changes -- including when the change originates internally rather than from a client call.

Define what modes this runtime actually has. With a deterministic tool-router executor, plausible modes are things like a dry-run or read-only mode versus an execute mode; that would give the permission gating in Phase 4.1 something to key on. Do not invent modes with no behavioral difference.
acceptance_criteria: Available modes are defined with real behavioral differences and advertised at session creation; set_session_mode updates registry state and takes effect on the next turn; CurrentModeUpdate is emitted on every change including internal ones; tests cover switching mid-session and an invalid mode id.
notes: pyacp-hnk.4 recorded CurrentModeUpdate as DEFERRED to this bead in turns.SESSION_UPDATE_DISPOSITIONS. When session/set_mode lands: (1) emit CurrentModeUpdate after a successful Session.set_mode (which already validates the mode id and refuses a session with no modes); (2) change that row's disposition from DEFERRED to EMITTED -- tests/test_turns.py::test_the_deferred_variants_are_the_phase_5_ones asserts the deferred set is exactly {CurrentModeUpdate, ConfigOptionUpdate} and will fail until the table is updated; (3) NewSessionResponse.modes is None today, so something has to start offering modes for the method to be reachable at all.
close_reason: Three modes with real behavioural differences (execute/dry-run/auto-approve), declared on the executor like supported_prompt_blocks since only the executor can act on one; deep-copied per session because set_mode mutates in place. dry-run encodes 'skipped' as completed + absent rawOutput + a marker in content, because ACP's ToolCallStatus has no such value -- documented as a choice. current_mode_update goes through one door (agent.announce_mode) so an internal change is indistinguishable from a client-driven one. CurrentModeUpdate flipped DEFERRED -> EMITTED. 514 tests; verified over stdio.

title: Implement authenticate and logout flows
description:
initialize currently returns authMethods: [] and auth: {logout: null} -- we advertise no authentication at all. Decide whether this runtime has anything to authenticate: with no LLM and an MCP backend spawned locally, there may be no credential in the picture, in which case declining is the honest answer and this issue is about recording that decision, not writing an auth system.

If there IS something (a remote MCP backend over http/sse, for instance), implement authenticate and logout and populate authMethods for real.
acceptance_criteria: Either authenticate and logout are implemented with a populated authMethods list and tests, or the decision to decline authentication is recorded with a rationale and the capability block honestly reflects it; no aspirational literals either way.
notes: pyacp-4ns.2 (docs/acp-compliance-matrix.md) found 'logout' is unroutable at agent-client-protocol 0.12.1: AGENT_METHODS['logout'] and AgentAuthCapabilities.logout both exist, but build_agent_router registers no logout route and acp.interfaces.Agent has no logout member. Reachable only via ext_method or a hand-added route. The matrix advertises NO authMethods and leaves agentCapabilities.auth.logout null, so 'authenticate' is an explicit typed refusal and there is nothing to log out of. Recommended resolution: drop logout from this bead's scope; if it is kept, it must be justified against an auth method we actually offer.
close_reason: DECLINED, with the rationale recorded and bound to its premise. No credential exists: no LLM (D1), MCP backends are local subprocesses inheriting the user's own environment, and the three remote MCP transports are advertised false and refused at session/new. That third premise is the one that can rot, so a test asserts empty AUTH_METHODS and absent remote transports together -- flipping mcpCapabilities.http/.sse/.acp now fails until the decision is revisited (verified by flipping http). logout DROPPED FROM SCOPE per the matrix's recommendation: re-verified unrouted at SDK 0.12.1 (in AGENT_METHODS, no route, no Agent member), already pinned by the conformance suite. authenticate unchanged -- a typed -32000 refusal since tzd.1. No aspirational literals either way. 532 tests.

title: Call fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file, gated on client capability
description:
Consume the client's filesystem methods rather than touching the filesystem directly, so the client stays in control of what is read and written.

Gate on the clientCapabilities captured at initialize (Phase 1.4) and define the fallback when the client does not offer fs -- direct filesystem access, or refusal. That choice interacts with Phase 2.5's containment rule, which is where the directory boundary is enforced.

read_text_file takes optional line and limit parameters; support them rather than always reading whole files.
acceptance_criteria: Both methods called through the client when advertised; line and limit honored on read; behavior with no fs capability is defined, documented, and tested; paths respect Phase 2.5's containment rule; a client that errors on the call does not crash the turn.
notes:
pyacp-3rw.4 settled the containment rule this bead enforces. Do not re-derive it:

    from python_acp.paths import require_contained
    resolved = require_contained(path, session.roots, "fs/read_text_file path")

- session.roots is (cwd, *additional_directories), already validated absolute and
  lexically normalised at the edge in agent.py.
- require_contained returns the RESOLVED path; use it. Re-deriving from the original
  string would open something the check never saw.
- Both sides resolve symlinks. A link inside cwd pointing at /etc/shadow is refused; a
  link inside pointing back inside is allowed; a declared root that is itself a link is
  still a live boundary. A prefix match is NOT containment. Empty roots permits nothing.
- PathConstraintError subclasses ValueError, so errors.to_request_error already answers
  -32602 with the reason in data. No special case needed.

KNOWN LIMIT this bead inherits and may need to close: containment is a CHECK, NOT A LOCK.
Resolution happens at check time, so a path that passes can become a symlink out of the
tree a microsecond later (TOCTOU). Closing it needs the fd actually opened -- openat /
O_NOFOLLOW -- which belongs with the code doing the opening, i.e. here. Documented in
src/python_acp/paths.md under "What this does not promise".
pyacp-hnk.1: gating lives on the turn seam, not at each call site. Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.

RESOLVED (pyacp-8bv.2, in progress): the open question in the description -- "define the
fallback when the client does not offer fs: direct filesystem access, or refusal" -- is
answered REFUSAL. There is no direct-filesystem fallback and there will not be one.
Settled by pyacp-hnk.1's ClientGates ("Absent capabilities mean **no** ... which is the
only safe reading") and by this bead's own opening sentence: opening a file behind the
client's back defeats "so the client stays in control of what is read and written".

HOW the refusal is produced matters and is also settled: branch on context.allows(gate)
at PARSE time and refuse the turn with TurnResult.refused() before anything runs.
Do NOT route the ordinary no-capability case through context.require(gate) --
UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 and means OUR conformance bug, so it
would report us as broken for a client's perfectly conforming absence of a capability.
require() is kept at the call site as an assertion, where a shut gate really would mean
the parse-time check was missing.

ALSO FOUND: the KNOWN LIMIT this bead was told it "may need to close" (containment is a
check, not a lock; TOCTOU) CANNOT be closed here, and the premise that it could was
wrong. paths.md said the openat/O_NOFOLLOW fix "belongs with the code doing the opening,
i.e. Phase 4.2". Phase 4.2 opens nothing -- the CLIENT opens the file, over the wire.
The mitigation available on this side is sending the resolved path so the client is not
asked to re-walk links already walked; the rest is the client's fs/* implementation.
paths.py, paths.md and turn_mcp_router.md now say so.
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met; merged to main. fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file called through the client, gated with allows() at parse time (refusal) and require() at the call site as our-invariant assertion; line/limit honored; containment via require_contained with the resolved path. Verified in-process and over a real pipe in the interop client. 604 tests pass.

title: Call the terminal/* client method family
description:
Consume create_terminal, terminal_output, wait_for_terminal_exit, kill_terminal, and release_terminal.

Terminals are stateful and leak: a created terminal must be released on every path including turn cancellation, session close (Phase 2.3), and client disconnect. Track live terminals per session so cleanup is possible.

output_byte_limit exists on CreateTerminalRequest for a reason -- unbounded output is a real failure mode. Set it.
acceptance_criteria: All five methods callable and gated on client capability; every created terminal is released on normal completion, cancellation, session close, and disconnect; live terminals tracked per session; output_byte_limit set to a documented default; tests cover the leak paths, not just the happy path.
notes:
pyacp-hnk.1: gating lives on the turn seam, not at each call site. Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.
CORRECTION (2026-08-23), supersedes the "Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X)" line above. That guidance is hnk.1-era and predates pyacp-8bv.2, which established the split now in force:

  • context.allows(Gate.TERMINAL) at PARSE time -> a client that never advertised terminal gets TurnResult.refused(). This is the ordinary case and is NOT our bug.
  • context.require(Gate.TERMINAL) survives at the CALL SITE as an assertion of our own invariant -- parsing should already have refused, so reaching a client method ungated really is a conformance bug and -32603 is honest there.

Following the stale line literally reports -32603 for the ordinary "client does not do terminals" case, which lies to the client about whose fault it is. See src/python_acp/turn_mcp_router.py (_reads/_writes) and turns.md for the shape to copy. Still accurate from the original note: TERMINAL is ONE boolean for all five terminal/* methods -- no per-method granularity exists.

DISCONNECT, resolved (2026-08-23): the acceptance criterion "every created terminal is released on ... disconnect" cannot be met literally. Terminals live in the CLIENT; once it disconnects there is nobody to send terminal/release to. Sessions deliberately survive disconnect (sessions.py:368 -- a disconnecting client must not silently delete sessions another connection may use). Decision: on disconnect, DROP OUR TRACKING so we do not leak memory, and state plainly in the module doc that the terminals themselves are the departed clients to reap. Do not pretend to release them.

PATTERN, decided (2026-08-23): mirror src/python_acp/mcp_registry.py rather than inventing a second lifecycle shape. It already solves this: per-session tracking, close(session_id) wired to the SessionRegistry.on_close hook, close_all() for process shutdown with the explicit "not for a disconnect" distinction, and remove-the-entry-BEFORE-stopping ordering so a teardown that raises cannot leave a session addressable with dead resources.
close_reason: Merged to main. All five terminal/* methods callable and gated (allows-at-parse, require-at-call-site); per-session TerminalRegistry mirroring mcp_registry; released on completion, cancellation, and session close; disconnect drops tracking and releases nothing, as decided and documented. output_byte_limit defaults to 1 MiB, derived from the 8 MiB MCP stream limit. 664 tests pass; leak paths covered against real subprocesses.

title: Handle all ACP content block types with capability gating
description:
Handle TextContentBlock, ImageContentBlock, AudioContentBlock, ResourceContentBlock, and EmbeddedResourceContentBlock on the way in.

The current initialize advertises promptCapabilities image, audio, and embeddedContext all false. Whatever this issue actually implements determines which of those literals flip -- and per Phase 1.4, a literal cannot be flipped without a feature test behind it. Declining a block type is a legitimate outcome as long as advertisement matches.
acceptance_criteria: Every content block type either handled or explicitly declined with the correct error; promptCapabilities literals match implemented behavior exactly; a client sending a declined type gets a clear error rather than a crash or silent drop; tests cover each type.
notes: pyacp-hnk.2: turn_mcp_router only reads block.text, so an image or audio prompt block is refused today with an agent_message_chunk naming the convention -- which is exactly what promptCapabilities.image/.audio/.embeddedContext being false promises. This bead flips those literals, and each flip needs a CAPABILITY_EVIDENCE entry in tests/test_capabilities.py naming the test that proves the block type is genuinely handled; the suite fails otherwise. The refusal text comes from turn_mcp_router.CONVENTION.
close_reason: All five prompt block types handled: text read, the other four DECLINED BY NAME with a stated reason (each is context for a model and D1 puts none here). promptCapabilities.image/.audio/.embeddedContext are now DERIVED from TurnExecutor.supported_prompt_blocks rather than written in the manifest, so the advertisement cannot drift from the executor in either direction -- which matters because D3 makes the executor swappable. Finding: resource_link is governed by NO capability at all (PromptCapabilities has 3 fields, the union has 4 non-text types), so its refusal carries its own reason; pinned by a test. 392 tests; verified end-to-end over stdio.

title: Implement the extended lifecycle: load_session, resume_session, fork_session, list_sessions, close_session
description:
The optional-but-required-for-strict-full-v1 lifecycle surface. Depends on Phase 2.1's copy-versus-share decisions.

fork_session is in the SDK's Agent protocol and was ABSENT from the original plan -- do not skip it.

Each method implemented here must flip its corresponding literal in the initialize capability block (loadSession, sessionCapabilities.delete, and so on), per Phase 1.4's rule that advertisement matches reality.
acceptance_criteria: All five methods implemented against the SDK models; each has its capability literal flipped in initialize and a test proving the feature; load and resume restore session metadata and backends correctly; fork produces an independent session per the documented semantics; list_sessions paginates via cursor; close_session releases MCP backends and terminals.
notes:
pyacp-4ns.2: close_session, fork_session, and resume_session are unstable-gated in the SDK. They are unreachable unless pyacp-tzd.1 built the connection with use_unstable_protocol=True. Verify that before implementing. fork_session was absent from the original plan and must not alias the parent session's mutable state.
pyacp-3rw.1 findings, for this bead to consume:

1. acp.contrib.session_state was evaluated and REPLACED for the registry (wrong direction:
   it consumes SessionNotifications a client receives; single-session; no cwd/dirs/config/
   timestamps/lifetime; marked experimental). BUT SessionAccumulator is a good fit for the
   HISTORY half of load_session -- feed it every SessionNotification the session sends and
   it holds the replay in a form the SDK maintains. Weigh the experimental marker before
   depending on it. See src/python_acp/sessions.md.
2. Fork/resume semantics are FIXED in sessions.py, do not rediscover them: fork = new id +
   deep copy of modes/config (they are mutated in place, a shallow copy aliases) + its own
   MCP backend instances + starts idle; resume = same object, shares everything, touch()
   only. A shared backend would make close on the fork tear down the parent's tools; a
   refcounted share is a valid optimisation only if close-independence survives.
3. SessionRegistry.list() already fixes the ordering (updated_at desc, session_id tiebreak)
   so a cursor means the same thing to every caller. Pagination itself is this bead's.
4. SessionRegistry(on_close=...) is the seam for mcp_registry teardown -- awaited with the
   session id after the entry is removed. sessions.py deliberately never imports MCP
   (module-boundaries B6a).
5. Advertising sessionCapabilities.list / .fork / .resume / .close and loadSession means
   flipping rows in capabilities.AGENT_CAPABILITY_MANIFEST *and* adding entries to
   CAPABILITY_EVIDENCE in tests/test_capabilities.py naming the tests that prove them.

title: Make the Makefile venv handling correct both in an activated venv and on a bare CI runner
description:
The Makefile assumes one environment shape and silently does the wrong thing in the other.

Local (this sandbox and any developer who has run 'source venv/bin/activate'): VIRTUAL_ENV=/Users/dave/dev/other/python-acp/venv and PATH starts with venv/bin, so the Makefile's 'PYTHON ?= python3' resolves to venv/bin/python3 -- the interpreter inside the venv make is about to manage. VENV_DIR resolves to 'venv' because that directory exists.

GitHub Actions (all four legs of the ci.yml matrix added in pyacp-0f6): a fresh checkout has neither .venv nor venv, so VENV_DIR falls through to '.venv', no venv is active, and 'python3' is whatever actions/setup-python put on PATH.

Concrete defects that follow:

1. 'make venv' never recreates an existing venv -- the recipe is guarded by 'if [ ! -d $(VENV_DIR) ]'. So 'make venv PYTHON=python3.12' on a machine that already has venv/ built from 3.14 does not build a 3.12 environment; it pip-installs into the 3.14 one and reports success. There is no supported way to reproduce a non-default matrix leg locally. Validating pyacp-0f6 required building .venv311/.venv312/.venv313 by hand, entirely outside the Makefile, precisely because of this.

2. VENV_DIR differs between the two environments ('venv' locally, '.venv' in CI) purely as a side effect of which directory happens to exist. Two developers on the same commit can be using different directories, and neither matches CI.

3. Every target depends on venv, and the venv recipe unconditionally runs 'pip install --upgrade pip' followed by 'pip install -e .[dev]'. So 'make test' always reaches the network. In a network-restricted sandbox that is a hard failure (pip cannot verify the proxy's TLS cert against Python's CA store, so make venv exits non-zero before any test runs); in CI it is wasted time on every invocation.

4. DEMO_MCP_COMMAND defaults to bare 'python3 tests/fixtures/mock_mcp_server.py' rather than $(PYTHON_BIN). 'make run' therefore launches the MCP subprocess on whatever python3 is on PATH while the bridge itself runs on $(VENV_DIR)/bin/python. Those coincide only when a venv is already activated -- exactly the local case, which is why it has never been noticed.
design:
Make the environment explicit instead of inferred.

- Pin VENV_DIR to a single default ('.venv') rather than deriving it from whichever directory exists, and keep it overridable. Decide what to do about the existing venv/ (support both for a transition, or document the rename).
- Make the venv recipe version-aware: record the interpreter used to build it (a stamp file, or read $(VENV_DIR)/bin/python --version) and rebuild when $(PYTHON) does not match, so 'make venv PYTHON=python3.12 VENV_DIR=.venv312' is the supported way to reproduce a matrix leg.
- Gate the pip install behind that stamp so lint/test/build stop hitting the network on every run; add an explicit 'make sync' or force flag for when deps genuinely changed.
- Point DEMO_MCP_COMMAND at $(PYTHON_BIN).
- If PYTHON resolves inside VENV_DIR itself (the activated-venv case), resolve it to the base interpreter or fail with a clear message rather than bootstrapping a venv from inside the venv it is replacing.

Verify by running the same make targets in both shapes: with venv activated, and in a container or fresh clone with no venv present.
acceptance_criteria: 'make venv PYTHON=<other-interpreter>' produces an environment on that interpreter even when a venv already exists, and every matrix leg from ci.yml is reproducible locally with a documented one-line command; 'make lint' and 'make test' succeed with no network access once the venv is provisioned; 'make run' launches the MCP subprocess on the venv interpreter; all four ci.yml legs stay green; CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md describe the venv contract, including which directory is canonical.

title: A forwarded elicitation carries no toolCallId, so a client cannot attach the question to the tool call that provoked it
description:
ElicitationFormSessionMode takes an optional toolCallId, and elicitation.py leaves it unset.

A client rendering the form therefore shows it detached from the tool call it belongs to -- which is exactly the case the field exists for: an MCP server asks for input in the middle of a tools/call, and the UI should attach the question to that call's entry rather than float it beside the transcript.

The id is known where it is needed and not where it is used. turn_mcp_router._run emits the ToolCallStart and holds the id; the elicitation handler runs on MCPStdioClient's read-loop dispatch, in a task of its own, with no link back to the caller. contextvars do not cross that boundary, because the task is created from the read loop rather than from the caller.

Options to weigh:

1. Track the in-flight tool call per (backend, request id). mcp_stdio knows which of OUR requests are outstanding; an elicitation arriving while exactly one tools/call is in flight on that backend is almost certainly about it. 'Almost certainly' is the weakness -- concurrent calls on one backend make it a guess, and a wrong toolCallId is worse than none.
2. Have the router register the current tool call id on the session before calling, and have the forwarder read it. Correct only while a session runs one turn at a time, which sessions.py does enforce (TurnAlreadyRunningError) -- but a turn may run several invocations, and only sequentially today.
3. Leave it unset. Honest, and what ships now.

Option 2 looks strongest given the one-turn-at-a-time rule, but it puts turn state somewhere the read loop can see it, which is a real coupling to design rather than to bolt on.
acceptance_criteria: Either a forwarded elicitation carries the toolCallId of the invocation that provoked it, with a test proving it is the right one and not merely present, or the decision to leave it unset is recorded in elicitation.md with the reasoning that settles it.
notes: discovered-from: pyacp-8bv.4

title: A malformed mcpServers entry is silently dropped, so session/new can hand back a session whose tools do not exist
description:
The SDK parses session/new's mcpServers with skip_invalid_items, so an entry that does not match McpServerStdio (a typo'd key, a missing command) is removed from the list BEFORE PythonAcpAgent.new_session is called. The agent then opens the servers that survived, succeeds, and returns a sessionId. The client asked for N servers and got a session backed by fewer, with no error and no warning.

That is precisely the failure mcp_registry's all-or-nothing opening exists to prevent -- 'a partially-opened session would hand back an id whose tools silently do not exist' -- arriving by a route mcp_registry cannot see, because by then the entry is gone.

Made visible by pyacp-6ni.3: tests/test_negative.py::test_a_malformed_mcp_server_entry_is_dropped_not_refused pins it as current behaviour so an SDK change is noticed, but pinning is not fixing.

Options, none of them free:
1. Compare counts at the transport. transport_ws.py still has the raw dict before the SDK decodes it; it could count params.mcpServers and hand the agent the raw length, or refuse when the parsed list is shorter. Costs a layering violation -- the transport would need to know which method carries which list -- and does nothing for stdio unless duplicated there.
2. Ask the SDK to stop salvaging. Whether skip_invalid_items is configurable per call site is unknown; agent-client-protocol is pre-1.0 and this may be worth an upstream issue.
3. Accept it and document it in the README, on the grounds that a client sending a malformed server spec has a bug of its own. Weakest option: the whole point of the all-or-nothing rule is that silent partial success is worse than loud failure.

Related SDK-salvage behaviour: a junk protocolVersion becomes the default rather than -32602 (also pinned in test_negative.py). That one is benign by comparison -- the client learns the negotiated version in the reply.
acceptance_criteria: Either session/new refuses a request whose mcpServers contained an unparseable entry, or the decision to accept it is recorded with its reasoning in agent.md and the README; the pinning test is updated to match whichever holds.
notes: Do not 'fix' this by removing the pinning test. The test is what makes the behaviour visible; if the decision is to accept the salvage, the test stays and its docstring records why.
close_reason:
Closed with the decision recorded: the drop is ACCEPTED, and the reasoning is the protocol's, not convenience.

The bead listed three options and judged 'accept and document' the weakest. That judgement was made without the decisive fact: skip_invalid_items restores the ACP schema's own x-deserialize-skip-invalid-items annotation, and the schema carries it on 35 FIELDS -- mcpServers on all four session methods, plus additionalDirectories, availableModes, configOptions, content, locations, authMethods and more -- beside 84 fields marked x-deserialize-default-on-error. That is a deliberate protocol-wide posture: drop what you cannot parse rather than failing the message. Refusing here would not close a gap; it would be one agent opting out of ACP's robustness rule on one field, and doing it consistently would mean opting out on all 35.

Option 1 (compare counts at the transport) is also unavailable in practice, and for a stronger reason than the bead gave: acp.router validates inside its own wrapper, so NO ACP method can see raw params, and the only place holding the original dict is transport_ws.receive(). transport_stdio has no equivalent seam -- the SDK owns that read loop -- so the fix would work on WebSocket and not stdio. Behaviour that depends on how a client connected is worse than a documented limitation.

DELIVERED, because 'accept' should not mean 'do nothing'. The one place a client feels this is naming an absent server in a prompt, where 'this session opened [x]' reads like their own typo. That refusal now names the dropped-entry possibility and the four required fields. Also found: all four of name/command/args/env are required with no defaults, so a plausible entry like {name, command} is dropped exactly like nonsense -- pinned by a new test using that realistic shape.

Recorded in agent.md (with why refusing was rejected and where it could not be done) and README (a call-out telling clients to send all four fields, args and env as [] when empty). Pinning tests kept and their docstrings now carry the decision, so an SDK bump that stops salvaging re-opens it deliberately.

Also fixed en route: three README examples still passed --mcp-command after pyacp-sld.4 removed it, and the container example pointed at /app/mock_mcp_server.py -- a path Containerfile never copied, so that example had been broken independently of the flag.

title: A turn cancelled during terminal/create leaks a terminal we never learned the id of
description: If a turn is cancelled after the client has started the process but before the terminal/create response arrives, we never learn the terminal id, so it cannot be released or tracked. This is the ordinary lost-reply problem and no code on our side can close it; documented in terminals.md under 'The window this does not close'. Filed so it is tracked rather than only narrated. Possible mitigations to evaluate: shield the create call itself, or reconcile against a client-side terminal list if ACP ever offers one.

title: A turn outlives the session/prompt request that died
description:
agent.prompt's 'except asyncio.CancelledError' branch cancels the turn task and re-raises without awaiting it, so between the request dying and the task's next await the executor can still emit session/update notifications for a request nobody is reading. Not the same hole as pyacp-hnk.5's 'nothing emits after the response' guarantee, which is structural: on the normal path the response is built only after asyncio.wait({turn}) returns, so nothing can follow it. This is the no-response path.

Deliberately left alone in pyacp-hnk.5: awaiting the turn inside a cancelled request is how you turn a dead request into a hang if an executor ignores cancellation, and no shipped executor emits after being cancelled. Options if it ever matters: await the task under a short asyncio.wait_for so the window is bounded, or have TurnContext refuse to emit once its turn is detached. The second is enforcement rather than a convention, but it makes a late emit raise inside a detached task.

Reproduce: an executor that emits from an 'except CancelledError' handler under asyncio.shield, with the session/prompt request itself cancelled (not session/cancel).
close_reason: TurnContext.detach() in prompt's finally; emit raises DetachedTurnError afterwards. Chose the bead's second option (enforcement) over the bounded wait_for, since shield defeats any convention. session/cancel path unaffected and guarded by a test. Verified by removing the fix: 3 of 4 new tests fail.

title: MCP tool annotations would let permission distinguish reads from deletes
description: turn_mcp_router asks the client for permission before EVERY tool call, because MCP 2024-11-05 has no tool annotations and there is no way to tell a read from a delete. readOnlyHint / destructiveHint / idempotentHint / openWorldHint arrive in MCP 2025-03-26. If _SUPPORTED_MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS ever widens to include a revision that has them, the router can skip the prompt for readOnlyHint tools and mark destructiveHint ones more prominently. Blocked on the protocol-version bump, not on a heuristic -- see .claude/skills/mcp-protocol/spec-versions.md before widening the pin.
close_reason: Unblocked and done: the bead said 'blocked on the protocol-version bump', but pyacp-pb7 already moved the pin to 2025-06-18 for elicitation and annotations arrived in 2025-03-26. New mcp_tools.py maps readOnlyHint/destructiveHint/openWorldHint onto ACP ToolCall.kind, with a per-turn tools/list cache (lazy per server, best-effort for kinds, strict for available_commands). REFUSED the bead's suggestion to skip the prompt for readOnlyHint tools: a server asserting read-only to escape the permission prompt is a privilege escalation written by the party being restrained, and MCP's own spec says never to make tool-use decisions on annotations. A hint relabels the question; it never withdraws it. Two mapping decisions recorded: unstated hints stay 'other' EXCEPT destructiveHint, where MCP's true default means 'assume the worst' and feeds a warning; and destructive rounds to 'delete' rather than 'edit' because understating risk in a permission prompt is the worse error. Behaviour change: announce-tools no longer avoids every tools/list -- a turn still lists the servers it calls. Option description and its test docstring corrected; three golden transcripts re-recorded (diff read: kind other->read on the tool_call AND on the permission request, which is still sent).

title: Carry the legacy MCP passthrough methods on ext_method during the transition
description:
The JSON-RPC surface today includes direct MCP passthrough -- tools/list, tools/call, prompts/list, prompts/get, resources/list, resources/read -- which are MCP method names, not ACP ones. They do not belong in an ACP agent's method table once dispatch comes from acp.agent.router.

The SDK's Agent protocol has ext_method and ext_notification precisely as the escape hatch for non-spec methods. Move the passthrough there under a namespaced prefix, so it stays available through the migration without polluting the ACP surface.

Decide whether passthrough survives removal at all, or whether tool access should go exclusively through session/prompt once the tool-router executor exists.
acceptance_criteria: MCP passthrough reachable via ext_method under a documented namespace; no MCP method names remain in the ACP method table; existing consumers have a documented migration path; the long-term fate of passthrough is decided and recorded.
close_reason:
Closed as DECLINED, with the decision recorded rather than the move made. The bead asked for two things: move the MCP passthrough onto ext_method under a namespace, and decide whether passthrough survives at all. The second answer settles the first -- it does not survive, so the move is churn that would cost clients two breaking changes instead of one.

Three reasons: (1) the passthrough addresses the process-wide --mcp-command server, the exact arrangement ACP v1 inverted, so a namespaced _tools/call would preserve the pre-v1 architecture behind a new name and keep --mcp-command alive to serve it; (2) two breaking changes for a surface being deleted either way; (3) the bead's stated motive -- 'MCP method names do not belong in the ACP method table' -- is already satisfied, because transport_ws.receive() intercepts them before the SDK sees them and they were never in the router's table.

Confirmed with the user: passthrough dies with the legacy surface; no known consumers.

DELIVERED, because the old plan had put a false promise on the wire: ACTION_REPLACEMENTS named JSON-RPC targets (list_tools -> tools/list) that now die in the same release, so it was telling clients to migrate to something that disappears with them. It now names the ACP path (session/new + session/prompt) for the two actions that have one, and None for the five that do not -- MCP prompts, resources, and ping have no ACP counterpart. deprecation_notice omits 'use' for those; warn_deprecated gained a third branch so an operator is told the capability goes away, not just the spelling. README migration table rewritten to say what is lost. Recorded in legacy_ws.py/.md, agent.py/.md, docs/acp-compliance-matrix.md, docs/module-boundaries.md, docs/full-apc-plan.md 7.2, and pyacp-sld.3's notes.

title: Abstract the backend so non-MCP executors are possible
description:
Original plan item 6.3. Largely satisfied by Phase 3.1's TurnExecutor interface -- the point of that seam is that MCP stops being the only thing a turn can drive.

This issue is the remainder: make sure nothing MCP-specific leaks through the session registry, the capability advertisement, or the update-emission path, so that a second backend could be added without touching them. Verify by writing a trivial non-MCP executor as a test double rather than by inspection.

Reassess after Phase 3.1 lands -- this may close as already-done.
acceptance_criteria: No MCP-specific types appear in the session registry, capability block, or update emission path; a non-MCP test-double executor runs a complete turn end to end; if Phase 3.1 already achieved this, the issue closes with that finding recorded.
close_reason: Closed as already-achieved, with the finding proved rather than asserted. The TurnExecutor seam from Phase 3.1 IS the backend abstraction; no second one was added. tests/test_executor_neutrality.py: a complete non-MCP executor (declares all three descriptive attributes, emits real session/updates, reads its own mode) serves create -> set_mode -> prompt -> close through the SDK router; an AST walk holds sessions.py, capabilities.py and turns.py free of any backend import; build_agent_capabilities' signature is pinned so the block cannot learn about a backend. Two things examined and judged NOT leaks: session/new opens the client's mcpServers whatever executor is wired in (mcpServers is an ACP request parameter -- an LLM executor would want them too), and agentCapabilities.mcpCapabilities is an ACP-defined field every agent answers. Recorded in turns.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, and plan item 6.3.

title: Drive elicitation/create and elicitation/complete
description:
Consume the client's elicitation flow so the runtime can ask the user a structured question mid-turn.

This is also the ACP side of pyacp-pb7: an MCP server can send elicitation/create to us as its client, and the natural implementation is to forward it to the ACP client's elicitation flow. That forwarding is the strongest argument for declaring the elicitation capability in the MCP initialize request, and it requires bumping the pinned MCP protocol version to 2025-06-18. Sequence this issue with pyacp-pb7 deliberately.

Note create_elicitation is a request and complete_elicitation is a notification -- different shapes.
acceptance_criteria: Both elicitation methods driven correctly, gated on client capability; an MCP-server-initiated elicitation/create can be forwarded to the ACP client and its answer returned to the MCP server; the relationship to pyacp-pb7 is resolved rather than duplicated; tests cover forwarding and the no-capability path.
notes: pyacp-hnk.1: gating lives on the turn seam, not at each call site. Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.
close_reason: Elicitation forwarding lands: elicitation.py turns an MCP server's elicitation/create into an ACP form-mode, session-scoped one and hands the answer back. complete_elicitation declined structurally (elicitationId exists only on the URL variants, and nothing here creates one). Gate.ELICITATION split into ELICITATION_FORM/ELICITATION_URL -- ElicitationCapabilities is a container, not the marker the docs claimed.
